documents.title: ETFAD EADV position paper management of atopic dermatitis

chunks.content: Introduction Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disorder marked by intense itching (pruritus), dry skin (xerosis), and recurrent eczematous lesions. It affects both children and adults, with a lifetime prevalence of up to 20% in industrialized countries, and has a significant impact on physical, psychological, and socio-economic well-being [ , ]. AD is associated with an increased risk of comorbidities such as food allergies, asthma, allergic rhinitis, and mental health disorders [ , ]. The pathophysiology of AD is complex, involving genetic predisposition (notably mutations affecting the skin barrier), immune system dysregulation (especially T-cell driven and type-2 inflammation), and environmental factors [ – ]. Current AD management is stratified by severity, aiming to restore barrier function, control inflammation, and alleviate pruritus. For mild-to-moderate AD, treatment generally focuses on maintaining skin barrier function and controlling inflammation. Regular use of emollients is recommended for all patients, while topical anti-inflammatory agents – most commonly corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors – are applied to manage flares. In cases where symptoms are more persistent or frequent, systemic corticosteroids, antibodies against interleukins 4 and 13 or JAK inhibitors, and phototherapy may be considered [ ]. Proactive topical strategies with corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors are also recommended to reduce symptom recurrence and maintain long-term skin health [ , ]. Despite the effectiveness of topical corticosteroids, prolonged or extensive use may cause adverse effects, most notably skin atrophy [ ], as well as other cutaneous reactions as striae (stretch marks), telangiectasia (visible blood vessels), purpura (easy bruising), rosacea, perioral dermatitis, acne, hypertrichosis (excess hair growth), pigmentation change [ ], and increased skin pH favouring pathogenic colonization [ , ]. In addition, extended use of corticosteroids (more than 90 days per year) is strongly associated with increased risks of several serious systemic adverse outcomes, including bone fractures, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, myocardial infarction, and cataracts [ ]. There is also a risk of contact sensitization (allergic reactions to the steroid itself), which is more common than often recognized [ ]. These limitations highlight the need for supportive, well-tolerated adjunctive strategies that help maintain barrier function and may reduce reliance on pharmacologic therapy in patients with mild-to-moderate AD. Emerging evidence suggests that collagen turnover is impaired in AD and highlights the potential of collagen supplementation to modulate inflammation and support epidermal barrier function [ ]. Preclinical studies support these findings, demonstrating anti-inflammatory and barrier-restoring effects of orally administered collagen peptides in animal models and cell cultures, and showing reduced inflammation and dermatitis severity in atopic models [ , ]. Clinical studies in healthy and photo-damaged skin populations show that specific bioactive collagen peptides (BCPs) support skin regeneration, hydration, and elasticity [ – ], providing translational rationale for their application in barrier-impaired conditions such as AD. Two small trials showed that oral collagen peptide supplementation can reduce disease severity, improve barrier function and skin hydration, and decrease Th2 inflammation markers [ , ]. In Lee et al. [ ], a combination of hydrolysed collagen, hyaluronic acid, and proteoglycans was used, but treatment lasted only 4 weeks and lacked a placebo control. Although in Hakuta et al. [ ], oral collagen tripeptide was administered as a single intervention over 12 weeks, the absence of a placebo arm still prevents confirmation of the isolated contribution of collagen peptides. Given the limited evidence from single-arm trials, this randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluates 12-week oral supplementation of specific BCP in moderate AD, generating evidence on efficacy and providing sufficient insight for both clinical interpretation and the design of a larger follow-up trial. Methods Experimental Design and Participants The study was conducted as a monocentric, prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial in the Clinical Research Center (CRC) of Kiel, Germany. The primary object of this study was to investigate the effects of a specific BCP on symptom control and overall skin condition in patients with moderate AD. For ethical reasons, the concomitant use of a corticosteroid-containing cream (Volon A, triamcinolone acetonide), serving as rescue medication, and a body lotion ( Unguentum leniens ) was permitted. Consequently, particular attention was given to differences in the use of rescue medication between treatment groups and to the potential pathways linking treatment exposure with these outcomes, as rescue medication can directly influence symptom management and overall clinical outcomes [ – ]. A total of 30 participants with moderate AD were enrolled in the randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Fifteen participants were assigned to the collagen peptide group (CP-G) and 15 to the placebo group (P-G), with each participant receiving either a daily dose of 5 g of BCP or the matching placebo. Before any study-related procedures, the investigator provided detailed information to the participants about the study, including the potential benefits and risks of participation. symptom management and overall clinical outcomes [ – ]. A total of 30 participants with moderate AD were enrolled in the randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Fifteen participants were assigned to the collagen peptide group (CP-G) and 15 to the placebo group (P-G), with each participant receiving either a daily dose of 5 g of BCP or the matching placebo. Before any study-related procedures, the investigator provided detailed information to the participants about the study, including the potential benefits and risks of participation. The sample size for this exploratory trial was pragmatically determined based on methodological recommendations for pilot and feasibility studies, which suggest approximately 10–40 participants per group depending on the study aim and desired precision. As this study was primarily intended to explore the effects of BCP on clinical outcomes and to provide preliminary estimates of variability, no formal power calculation was performed, and no single primary outcome was pre-specified. The chosen sample size of 15 participants per group was deemed sufficient to allow for initial evaluation of treatment effects, assessment of study procedures, and estimation of parameters to inform the design of future confirmatory trials [ – ]. Eligible participants were adults aged 18 years or older, of any sex, with a confirmed diagnosis of AD − a moderate SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) score between 15 and 40 − and the ability to provide written informed consent. Participants were also required to be in overall good health, both physically and mentally, and able to comply with study procedures and the predefined visit schedule. Exclusion criteria included the presence of other acute skin conditions (e.g., psoriasis, urticaria, parasitic infections such as mites, scabies, lice, or fleas) or other dermatological findings on the test areas (e.g., scars, sunburn, or moles), intensive natural or artificial UV exposure (e.g., solarium), food allergies or intolerances to any ingredients of the test products, gastrointestinal disorders, tattoos on the test areas, and recent use of topical medications on the test areas (within 6 weeks) other than the permitted corticosteroid-containing cream and the body lotion (see above). Systemic use of anti-inflammatory agents or antibiotics within 2 weeks was also exclusionary. Additional exclusions were pregnancy or breastfeeding, immunological disorders, severe health problems within the past 6 months (e.g., cancer, acute cardiovascular disorders, severe diabetes), alcohol or drug abuse, participation in other cosmetic or pharmaceutical studies within the preceding 2–4 weeks, recent intake of nutritional supplements (within 4 weeks), significant lifestyle or dietary changes during the study, use of leave-on or oily skin-cleansing products on the arms, and any intellectual or mental impairment that would prevent adherence to study instructions. Consistent with previous clinical studies of collagen peptides in AD [ ], the study spanned 12 weeks and included an initial screening visit, a baseline assessment, an interim visit after 4 weeks, and a final post-intervention visit at 12 weeks. The interim assessment was scheduled at 4 weeks to capture early responses to the intervention in patients with AD, allowing differentiation between initial and later effects of BCP administration [ , , , ]. All participants began the intervention simultaneously, and adherence to the study protocol and product use was monitored at each visit. On each measurement day, subjects were acclimatized to the indoor conditions (21.5°C, 50% ± 5% relative humidity) for at least 30 min. An overview of the study phases and the schedule of assessments is provided in . Efficacy Outcomes Given that rescue medication use may modify treatment effects [ – ], differences in the use of rescue medication, body lotion, and total topical product consumption between groups were monitored and analysed as efficacy endpoints. Transepidermal water loss (TEWL) was measured to assess skin barrier integrity using an open-chamber device (Tewameter ® , Courage + Khazaka electronic GmbH, Cologne, Germany) in accordance with standardized procedures [ ]. The probe contains two temperature and humidity sensors, and the difference in water vapor partial pressure between the sensors is used to calculate the water flux density. Values are expressed in grams per square meter per hour (g/m 2 /h). Anatomical site, skin temperature, and local microclimate were carefully controlled, and repeated measurements were performed on the same area to reduce intraindividual variability [ – ]. Probe application time, handling procedures, and calibration were rigorously standardized to ensure reliability and comparability of results [ , , ]. Elevated TEWL indicates impaired epidermal barrier function, as typically seen in AD, and allows for monitoring of disease severity and treatment response [ ]. Skin hydration was assessed using the Corneometer ® (Courage + Khazaka electronic GmbH, Cologne, Germany), which measures the electrical capacitance of the stratum corneum as an indicator of water content. Higher capacitance values reflect greater skin hydration [ ]. Elevated TEWL indicates impaired epidermal barrier function, as typically seen in AD, and allows for monitoring of disease severity and treatment response [ ]. Skin hydration was assessed using the Corneometer ® (Courage + Khazaka electronic GmbH, Cologne, Germany), which measures the electrical capacitance of the stratum corneum as an indicator of water content. Higher capacitance values reflect greater skin hydration [ ]. Measurements were conducted under the same standardized environmental conditions as TEWL to ensure comparability and minimize external influences such as ambient humidity, temperature, or contact pressure [ , ]. Skin surface pH was assessed using a planar glass electrode (flat-tip pH meter; Courage + Khazaka electronic GmbH, Cologne, Germany) in accordance with established standardized protocols. Measurements were performed under controlled environmental conditions [ ] to minimize the influence of sweat, sebum, and other factors that could affect accuracy. All assessments were performed on predefined skin sites following a fixed measurement protocol, with triplicate readings averaged for analysis to enhance precision and reduce measurement noise. The SCORAD index is a validated clinical tool developed in the 1990s to assess the severity of AD [ , ]. It combines three main components: the extent of skin involvement (measured using the rule of nines, scored 0–100), the intensity of six key lesion features (erythema, oedema/papulation, oozing/crusts, excoriations, lichenification, and dryness, each scored 0–3), and subjective symptoms (pruritus and sleep loss, each rated by the patient on a 10-cm visual analogue scale) [ , ]. The final SCORAD score is calculated as A/5 + 7B/2 + C, where A is extent, B is intensity (maximum 18), and C is subjective symptoms (maximum 20), with a total possible score of 103 [ , ]. In this scoring system, intensity contributes 60% to the total score, while extent and subjective symptoms each contribute about 20% [ ]. The SCORAD index is widely used in clinical trials and practice due to its reliability, validity, and ability to capture both objective and patient-reported aspects of AD severity [ ]. Another outcome is the 5-D Pruritus Scale − a validated, multidimensional tool specifically designed to assess changes in itch intensity over time, making it suitable as a primary outcome measure in clinical studies of chronic pruritus, including AD [ ]. This scale evaluates five domains: duration, degree, and direction of itching (each rated on a 1–5 scale), as well as disability (impact on sleep, leisure/social activities, housework/errands, and work/school) and distribution (body areas affected) [ ]. Its multidimensional structure allows for a comprehensive assessment of both the severity and the impact of pruritus on daily life. The 5-D Pruritus Scale has demonstrated high reliability, validity, and sensitivity to change across various patient populations and languages, correlating well with other itch intensity measures and quality of life indices [ – ]. It is, therefore, a robust tool for detecting clinically meaningful changes in itch intensity and related disability in intervention studies. Quality of life was assessed using the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), a validated, self-administered 10-item questionnaire with scores ranging from 0 to 30, where higher values indicate greater impairment [ , ]. A change of 4 points is considered the minimal clinically important difference for inflammatory skin conditions [ ]. Test Products The test product CURADERM ® used in this study was a specific BCP derived from bovine type I collagen through a complex multistep process, characterized by a high safety profile and composed of specific collagen peptides. The BCP product was provided by GELITA AG (Eberbach, Germany). It is clearly defined by a matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization mass spectrometry fingerprint, which identifies collagen peptides with an average molecular weight of less than 2.0 kDa. The placebo product, containing maltodextrin, was obtained through the enzymatic conversion of starch and provided by Cargill (Haubourdin, France). Both the test product and placebo were packaged in single-dose sachets for daily use. Each single-dose sachet was dissolved in 250 mL of water prior to consumption. To maintain blinding for both the investigator and participants, all sachets were identical in appearance, and the test and placebo products matched in taste and texture. Statistical Analysis The statistician performing the analyses was also blinded. Unblinding occurred only after data collection was completed and the database had been locked. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Endpoints in this study were pre-specified without hierarchical ordering. The statistical analyses aimed to explore the relationship between interventions, thereby providing a basis for interpretation of the results and for planning future studies. Statistical Analysis The statistician performing the analyses was also blinded. Unblinding occurred only after data collection was completed and the database had been locked. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Endpoints in this study were pre-specified without hierarchical ordering. The statistical analyses aimed to explore the relationship between interventions, thereby providing a basis for interpretation of the results and for planning future studies. Two-sided tests were applied throughout, with a significance threshold of α = 0.05. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test. As the dataset contained both normally and non-normally distributed variables, the appropriate statistical test – parametric or non-parametric – was applied to each variable according to its distribution. Baseline comparisons between groups were performed using independent sample t tests for normally distributed continuous variables or the Mann-Whitney U test when normality assumptions were not met. Categorical variables were compared using χ 2 or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. To evaluate the overall treatment effect across all efficacy outcomes, mean changes from baseline to post-intervention (12 weeks) were compared between the CP-G and P-G using a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). Pillai’s Trace was used for multivariate interpretation due to its robustness against violations of covariance equality assumptions. Univariate follow-up tests were conducted to further examine group differences for specific outcomes. Within-group changes over time (baseline, week 4, and week 12) were analysed using repeated measures ANOVA for normally distributed data, with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons to identify specific time points with significant changes. For non-normally distributed data, the Friedman test was applied, followed by Dunn-Bonferroni pairwise comparisons when the overall test was significant. Within-group comparisons of lesional versus non-lesional skin for hydration, TEWL, and pH at baseline, week 4, and week 12 were performed using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. Additionally, skin pH values were tested against the lower (4.5) and upper (5.5) bounds of the physiological reference range using a one-sample t test for normally distributed data or a one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test for non-normally distributed data. Rescue medication is increasingly recognized as a key mediator that can influence the relationship between treatment and clinical outcomes. Mediation analysis was therefore performed to clarify whether and how rescue medication use transmits or modifies the effect of the primary treatment on participant outcomes [ – ]. To allow comparability across different statistical procedures, all effect sizes were converted to Cohen’s d with correction according to Hedges for small samples. This provides a unified scale for interpretation, with conventional thresholds of d = 0.20, 0.50, and 0.80 representing small, medium, and large effects, respectively [ – ]. Results Subject Characteristics A total of 30 participants were enrolled in the study and randomized to either the CP-G or P-G. Over the 12-week study period, with an intermediate assessment at week 4, three participants were excluded from the per-protocol analysis due to lack of compliance: one participant from the P-G and two participants from the CP-G (shown in ). The final per-protocol population thus included 14 participants in the P-G and 13 participants in the CP-G. No adverse events related to the intervention were reported. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population are summarized in . In the present study population, most participants were classified as having intrinsic AD (21/27), whereas extrinsic AD was less frequent (6/27). Extrinsic subtypes are characterized by higher serum IgE levels and an allergy-associated Th2 immune profile, whereas intrinsic subtypes show normal to mildly elevated IgE levels and lacked clear allergen sensitization. Regarding skin barrier function, extrinsic AD is associated with a more generalized impairment, while intrinsic AD predominantly showed increased TEWL in lesional skin, with less pronounced alterations in non-lesional areas. Symptom Management Outcomes Analysis of corticosteroid rescue medication use revealed a significant difference in total consumption between groups over the study period (CP-G: 0.935 ± 1.42 g; P-G: 5.60 ± 7.82 g; p = 0.045; d = 0.847), indicating that participants in the CP-G required less rescue medication (shown in ). Consumption of topical care lotion (CP-G: 5.14 ± 5.46 g; P-G: 15.2 ± 19.4 g; p = 0.084; d = 0.721) and total cream usage (CP-G: 6.08 ± 1.73 g; P-G: 20.8 ± 6.83 g; p = 0.055; d = 0.807) showed non-significant trends favouring the CP-G (shown in ). Clinical Efficacy Given the significant group differences in rescue medication use, this variable was included in subsequent MANOVA to provide a more accurate estimate of the overall effect of the intervention on clinical outcomes. Additionally, rescue medication was incorporated as a mediator in the mediation analyses to assess its potential role in the relationship between treatment and clinical outcomes. Clinical Efficacy Given the significant group differences in rescue medication use, this variable was included in subsequent MANOVA to provide a more accurate estimate of the overall effect of the intervention on clinical outcomes. Additionally, rescue medication was incorporated as a mediator in the mediation analyses to assess its potential role in the relationship between treatment and clinical outcomes. Across all clinical and physiological outcome variables, MANOVA revealed no statistically significant multivariate effect of treatment (V = 0.388, F (7, 19) = 1.72, p = 0.164). Despite the lack of statistical significance, the large effect size ( d = 1.59) suggests a meaningful overall trend towards improved outcomes in the CP-G. Skin Physiology Outcomes Univariate follow-up tests for lesional skin outcomes showed a trend towards lower skin surface pH values in the CP-G ( F (1, 25) = 3.33, p = 0.080, d = 0.732) indicating a potentially beneficial effect on skin barrier condition. At baseline, pH values of lesional skin were significantly higher than those of non-lesional skin in both the P-G ( p = 0.009) and CP-G ( p = 0.050), reflecting barrier impairment in affected areas (shown in ). After the 12-week intervention, pH values of both non-lesional and lesional skin in the CP-G were within the physiological range (4.5–5.5), indicating stabilization of the skin acid mantle. In contrast, in the P-G, pH values of both non-lesional ( p = 0.032; d = 1.30) and lesional skin ( p = 0.030; d = 1.17) increased significantly over time, with lesional skin showing a significant deviation above the physiological range by week 12 ( p = 0.009). Lesional stratum corneum hydration ( F (1, 25) = 0.16, p = 0.694, d = 0.155), and lesional TEWL ( F (1, 25) = 1.91, p = 0.179, d = 0.553), did not show statistically significant differences between the CP-G and P-G. At baseline, hydration and TEWL values of lesional skin were significantly different from those of non-lesional skin in both the CP-G (hydration: p = 0.020; TEWL: p = 0.001) and P-G (hydration: p = 0.007; TEWL: p = 0.001). After the 12-week intervention, lesional skin in the CP-G improved significantly ( p = 0.040, d = 1.07) and reached levels comparable to non-lesional skin for hydration ( p = 0.207), indicating substantial improvement in skin hydration. In contrast, in the P-G, lesional skin remained significantly different from non-lesional skin ( p = 0.008) despite significant improvements over time ( p = 0.007, d = 1.38). For TEWL, intragroup analyses over the entire intervention period revealed a large, though non-significant, improvement for the CP-G ( p = 0.098, d = 0.975) from 27.8 ± 16.8 to 21.9 ± 11.0 g/m 2 /h, whereas the P-G exhibited significant decreases ( p = 0.008, d = 2.44) from 34.7 ± 18.0 to 23.0 ± 14.6 g/m 2 /h. Mediation analysis quantified the contribution of rescue medication to these changes with a significant indirect effect (ab = 2.82, 95% CI [0.17, 6.87]), indicating that the TEWL reduction observed in the P-G was largely driven by their higher use of rescue medication. Scatterplots visualize the relationship between rescue medication use and changes in lesional TEWL, hydration, and pH. Each point represents one participant, allowing treatment effects to be interpreted in the context of individual rescue use (shown in ). Points located to the left indicate low rescue medication use. For TEWL and pH, points below the zero line reflect an improvement, whereas for hydration, points above the zero line indicate an improvement. Participants in the CP-G cluster predominantly in the left area of each panel, demonstrating that they improved despite using very little rescue medication. In contrast, the P-G showed a broad distribution across both rescue use and outcomes, suggesting that higher rescue medication partially compensated for the lack of active treatment. Patient-Reported Outcomes (Questionnaires) Univariate follow-up tests for patient-reported outcomes, including the SCORAD scores, 5-D Pruritus Scale, and DLQI, did not reveal statistically significant differences between the CP-G and P-G over the 12-week intervention period (all p > 0.05). For the 5-D Pruritus Scale, the CP-G demonstrated a significant overall reduction ( p = 0.020, d = 1.44), with improvements already evident at week 4 ( p = 0.024, d = 1.49), whereas the P-G showed significant reductions only after 12 weeks (overall p = 0.017, d = 1.24). For the DLQI, the CP-G showed a large, non-significant improvement ( p = 0.144, d = 0.902), which was larger than that observed in the P-G ( p = 0.256, d = 0.659). For the 5-D Pruritus Scale, the CP-G demonstrated a significant overall reduction ( p = 0.020, d = 1.44), with improvements already evident at week 4 ( p = 0.024, d = 1.49), whereas the P-G showed significant reductions only after 12 weeks (overall p = 0.017, d = 1.24). For the DLQI, the CP-G showed a large, non-significant improvement ( p = 0.144, d = 0.902), which was larger than that observed in the P-G ( p = 0.256, d = 0.659). For SCORAD scores, changes from baseline to post-intervention did not reach significance in the CP-G ( p = 0.807, d = 0.408), whereas the P-G showed significant improvement over time ( p = 0.026, d = 1.15). Scatterplots of rescue medication versus patient-reported outcomes (shown in ) showed a distribution pattern similar to that observed for skin physiology parameters: participants in the CP-G generally maintained low rescue use across SCORAD, 5-D Pruritus, and DLQI scores, indicating that improvements were largely independent of rescue medication. In contrast, the P-G exhibited a broader distribution, suggesting that higher rescue medication partially contributed to the observed reductions. No mediation effects were observed for the SCORAD total score, 5-D Pruritus Scale, or DLQI. Discussion The primary aim of the present study was to evaluate the effects of 12-week-specific BCP supplementation on clinical symptoms and skin barrier physiology in individuals with moderate AD. Analysis of rescue medication use revealed a favourable pattern for the CP-G: participants receiving specific BCP required significantly less topical corticosteroid rescue therapy, alongside additional non-significant trends towards reduced topical care lotion and overall topical product use. These findings indicate that clinical symptom control in the CP-G was achieved with a lower need for adjunctive treatment. Although no statistically significant multivariate treatment effect was observed, the overall effect size indicated a meaningful trend favouring the CP-G. Across skin physiology parameters, physiological pH values were maintained in both lesional and non-lesional areas, suggesting that specific BCP supplementation can help preserve skin pH within normal ranges, whereas placebo supplementation was associated with increased pH values that exceeded the physiological range over time. In addition, lesional skin hydration in the CP-G improved throughout the intervention, ultimately reaching levels similar to those of non-lesional skin. For TEWL, both groups demonstrated reductions over the intervention period; however, mediation analyses revealed that improvements in the P-G were largely driven by higher use of rescue medication, whereas the CP-G maintained low rescue use while showing favourable TEWL development. This pattern might be indicative for a potential barrier-supportive effect of specific BCP supplementation that may help stabilize skin physiology independently of additional topical treatment. In healthy individuals, supplementation with collagen peptides or composite supplements containing collagen peptides has led to significant improvements in skin hydration and reductions in TEWL, indicating enhanced skin barrier function [ , ]. Although first indicative evidence points to an influence of dietary patterns and specific nutrients on skin pH [ , ], direct clinical evidence demonstrating an effect of collagen peptide supplementation on skin pH is currently lacking. Nevertheless, while direct evidence on pH modulation by collagen peptides is limited, improved skin barrier integrity may support maintenance of a more physiologically acidic skin surface, which is important for overall skin health [ – ]. In the context of AD, collagen peptides have demonstrated the ability to alleviate AD symptoms, reduce TEWL, and improve skin hydration in animal models [ , ] and human trials [ , ]. These effects are linked to the restoration of skin barrier proteins like filaggrin and the reduction of inflammatory proteins, which are crucial for managing AD [ , , , ]. Increased TEWL and higher skin pH are associated with AD flares and barrier dysfunction, so interventions that lower TEWL and support barrier repair, such as collagen peptide supplementation, may be particularly beneficial for AD patients [ ]. However, while the evidence for TEWL and hydration is strong, more research is needed to clarify the direct impact of collagen peptides on skin pH, especially in AD. These findings should be interpreted in light of the bioavailability of orally ingested collagen peptides and their metabolism during gastrointestinal digestion and hepatic first-pass passage. Pharmacokinetic studies show that orally ingested BCPs partially survive gastrointestinal and first-pass metabolism, appear in human blood and skin in intact forms, and are associated with dermatologic benefits [ – ]. Animal and in vitro gut-liver models further indicate systemic bioavailability, with peptide-specific differences in first-pass metabolism and reported bioavailability of up to approximately 20% for key collagen-derived peptides [ – ]. Accordingly, multiple randomized controlled trials using BCPs have demonstrated improvements in skin hydration, elasticity, and dermal matrix parameters, suggesting that first-pass metabolism does not preclude biologically relevant dermatologic effects at commonly used doses [ – , ]. Precise

Pharmacokinetic studies show that orally ingested BCPs partially survive gastrointestinal and first-pass metabolism, appear in human blood and skin in intact forms, and are associated with dermatologic benefits [ – ]. Animal and in vitro gut-liver models further indicate systemic bioavailability, with peptide-specific differences in first-pass metabolism and reported bioavailability of up to approximately 20% for key collagen-derived peptides [ – ]. Accordingly, multiple randomized controlled trials using BCPs have demonstrated improvements in skin hydration, elasticity, and dermal matrix parameters, suggesting that first-pass metabolism does not preclude biologically relevant dermatologic effects at commonly used doses [ – , ]. Precise tissue concentrations and the most active circulating peptide species represent a topic for ongoing investigation. Patient-reported outcomes pointed in a favourable direction for the CP-G: while between-group differences did not reach statistical significance, pruritus reductions emerged earlier and DLQI improvements showed larger effect estimates in the CP-G compared with placebo. In contrast, SCORAD improved mainly in the P-G, likely reflecting higher rescue medication use. Although the mediation analysis did not support rescue use as a significant mediator, exploratory visual inspection indicated that improvements in the CP-G tended to occur with consistently low rescue intake. These findings are generally in line with previous reports showing benefits of collagen peptide supplementation on patient- or clinician-reported measures reflecting overall disease improvement, such as SCORAD [ ] or Global Improvement Assessment scores [ ]. However, in contrast to Hakuta et al. [ ], SCORAD improvements were not observed in the CP-G here, which may be attributable to differences in rescue medication use. Importantly, the reduced reliance on corticosteroid rescue therapy in the CP-G has substantial clinical relevance, as prolonged or extensive use of topical corticosteroids is associated with multiple topical and systemic adverse effects as well as contact sensitization [ – ]. Therefore, interventions that reduce the need for corticosteroid use, such as collagen peptide supplementation, are important to minimize these risks and improve long-term safety for patients with AD. This trial has some limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. The relatively small sample size may have limited statistical power, which could explain the lack of some significant between-group differences despite meaningful effect sizes, highlighting the need for larger studies to confirm these findings. Differences in rescue medication use also influenced improvements in skin physiology and patient-reported outcomes; however, this underscores a clinically relevant observation, as participants in the CP-G achieved comparable or better effects while using substantially less corticosteroid therapy. While statistical adjustments were applied to account for these differences, the impact on outcomes remains unavoidable, since corticosteroid use could not be ethically restricted. Finally, the effects reported here are specific to the particular collagen peptide formulation used. Given that collagen peptides vary in composition, bioavailability, and mechanisms of action, these results cannot be generalized to all collagen supplements. In conclusion, the present findings provide first controlled evidence that specific BCPs (CURADERM ® ) may support barrier recovery, maintain physiological skin pH, and promote early symptom relief in mild-to-moderate AD. Notably, participants receiving BCP supplementation showed an earlier reduction in pruritus compared to placebo, suggesting a faster onset of symptom improvement. The overall reduction in corticosteroid rescue therapy use, alongside favourable trends in key physiological skin parameters, further supports the potential of specific BCPs as a safe and beneficial adjunct to standard care. These results warrant confirmation in larger, adequately powered trials designed to disentangle true treatment effects from concomitant rescue therapy use and to validate the observed early clinical response.
